meta.subsidies.html.title: Subsidies for hotels | Lemnion · Hospitality Energy Solutions | EIA · MIA · ISDE · SPRILA · ERE
meta.subsidies.html.description: Subsidies for hotels: EIA, MIA/Vamil, ISDE and SPRILA for EV chargers, batteries and solar panels. Plus ERE income per charged kWh. Lemnion handles the application.
subsidies.intro: The government encourages energy storage and sustainability with substantial subsidies. Lemnion helps your hotel benefit to the full, from application to payout.
subsidies.label: Keep reading
subsidies.h2: Up to 60% subsidy on your investment
subsidies.intro2: The Netherlands has several subsidy schemes specifically aimed at energy investments for businesses. By combining subsidies and tax deductions smartly, your hotel can recoup up to 60% of the investment.
subsidies.eia-p: Additional deduction on taxable profit for energy-saving business assets. Battery storage, EMS and charging infrastructure qualify.
subsidies.mia-p: MIA: up to 45% additional deduction (depending on the rank on the environmental list) on environmental investments. Vamil: 75% free depreciation, so you set the pace.
subsidies.mia-li1: MIA: up to 45% investment deduction (environmental list)
subsidies.mia-li2: Vamil: free depreciation on 75% of the investment
subsidies.mia-li3: Combinable with EIA for maximum benefit
subsidies.isde-p: Sustainable Energy Investment Subsidy for commercial users: (hybrid) heat pumps, solar water heaters and small wind turbines. Solar panels are not covered; for those, use the EIA.
subsidies.isde-li1: Subsidy on heat pumps, solar water heaters and small wind turbines
subsidies.sprila-label: Subsidy scheme for private charging infrastructure at companies
subsidies.sprila-p: Subsidy scheme for private charging infrastructure at companies: chargers on owned or leased premises for guests and staff. Ideal for hotels.
subsidies.sprila-li1: AC charging station ≥11 kW or DC charging station ≥20 kW
subsidies.sprila-li2: Own or leased premises, also for guests
subsidies.sprila-status: Reference date: 17-08-2026 · Open for applications · Budget €122.5m · Applications until 18-12-2026 · Source: RVO.nl
subsidies.ere-p: Not a subsidy, but an additional revenue stream: Emission Reduction Units (EREs) you earn per delivered kWh of green power to chargers. From 2026 the successor to HBEs. Tradable to fuel suppliers.
subsidies.ere-li2: Earn per kWh of green power to EVs
subsidies.ere-li3: Applies to all charging: staff and guests
subsidies.ere-li4: Tradable: fuel suppliers must surrender them before 1 April
subsidies.ere-status: 26-29 June 2026 · Source: Joulo via Duurzaam Ondernemen
subsidies.ere-tip: 💡 Not automatic: register the chargers through an NEa-recognised booking service provider | they arrange the NEa registration, audit and sale. Requirements: MID meter + verifiable green power.
subsidies.spula-label: Public Charging Infrastructure Subsidy, heavy transport
subsidies.spula-p: Subsidy scheme for public charging infrastructure in public spaces, specifically for heavy vehicles (trucks, freight traffic). Usually less relevant for hotels | the hotel scheme is SPRILA.
subsidies.spula-status: Reference date: 17-08-2026 · Open for applications until 18-12-2026 · Source: RVO.nl

subsidies.artikel-h2: EREs for hotels: the revenue stream behind your EV chargers
subsidies.artikel-h3-1: Your chargers cost money. Since 2026, they can also earn money.
subsidies.artikel-p1: Every hotel that installs EV chargers does the same calculation: the investment is substantial, the payback period is long, and guest demand grows faster than the budget. Since 1 January 2026, a new factor has changed that calculation: EREs. Emission Reduction Units, tradable certificates that are created with every kWh charged. For hotels with charging infrastructure, this means a recurring income stream of roughly €0.12 per charged kWh, fixed for all of 2026. At 100,000 kWh per year, that comes to around €12,000 to €13,000; with an own solar installation, it rises to around €20,000.
subsidies.artikel-p2: This article gives you the complete picture: what EREs are, how the scheme works, when you get paid, and why the combination with solar panels is especially attractive for hotels.
subsidies.artikel-h3-2: What EREs are, explained for a hotelier
subsidies.artikel-p3: ERE stands for Emission Reduction Unit. The system is operated in the Netherlands by the Dutch Emissions Authority (NEa) and started on 1 January 2026, succeeding the older HBE scheme.
subsidies.artikel-p4: How it works, in five steps:
subsidies.artikel-li1: Your charger delivers power to an electric car. The MID meter inside the charger records every kWh accurately.
subsidies.artikel-li2: A recognised booking service provider registers those kWhs with the NEa. The system converts them into EREs.
subsidies.artikel-li3: One ERE represents one kilogram of avoided CO2; a charged kWh represents roughly 0.5 ERE.
subsidies.artikel-li4: Fuel suppliers are legally required to surrender EREs for the fossil fuel they sell. That obligation is rising: 14.4% in 2026, 28.4% in 2030. They buy the EREs.
subsidies.artikel-li5: The revenue goes to the party that holds the energy contract for the connection: in a hotel's case, the hotel.
subsidies.artikel-p5: The logic is clear: the fossil sector finances the greening of transport, and hotels that make electric charging possible receive the value of it.
subsidies.artikel-li6: Every charger counts, whether for guests, staff or passers-by. Even a single charge point qualifies.
subsidies.artikel-li7: The former minimum threshold of about 200,000 kWh per year has been removed. For SMEs and hotels, there is no lower limit anymore.
subsidies.artikel-li8: The hard requirement is a MID meter inside the charger itself: an officially approved meter that measures what actually goes into the car. A loose meter in the meter cupboard does not qualify.
subsidies.artikel-li9: Registration and booking run exclusively through NEa-recognised booking service providers. The hotel does not need to do the administration itself; there is a mandatory annual verification.
subsidies.artikel-h3-4: How and when you get paid
subsidies.artikel-p7: The hotel authorises a booking service provider for at least one calendar year. That party handles the rest: reading out the charger (automatically via OCPP or through annual meter readings), booking in with the NEa, selling on the emissions market and paying out. Most providers pay quarterly, after verifying the figures; some pay annually.
subsidies.artikel-p8: The first payouts have already taken place: a 50% advance over Q1 2026 was paid in July. An important detail for hotels that have not registered yet: the scheme works retroactively to 1 January 2026. kWhs charged before you register also count. There is no maximum number of participants.
subsidies.artikel-callout1: Do factor in the mandatory annual verification. Its cost is typically between €150 and €750, depending on whether an on-site inspection is required.
subsidies.artikel-h3-5: How the market value is determined
subsidies.artikel-p9: EREs are not traded on a public exchange. The price is an OTC price: it is set in negotiated transactions between selling booking service providers and buying fuel suppliers.
subsidies.artikel-li10: One ERE trades around €0.46 to €0.50. The latest verified transactions (June 2026) were at €0.4775 and €0.481.
subsidies.artikel-li11: A charged kWh represents roughly €0.23 in gross market value (0.5 ERE per kWh × roughly €0.46, based on 100% counting).
subsidies.artikel-li12: On grid power, 50.5% of every kWh counts; after commission (typically 13% to 19%) that leaves roughly €0.10 to €0.13 net per kWh. For 2026, a level of around €0.12 per kWh is guaranteed by at least one major provider.
subsidies.artikel-li13: Fuel supplier obligations run until 2030, which supports the demand structure over time.
subsidies.artikel-p11: Because there is no public listing, we track the verified transaction prices. As soon as new transactions are known, we publish them on this page.
subsidies.artikel-h3-6: Why solar panels make the difference
subsidies.artikel-p12: Here is the most interesting part for hotels that have already invested in solar panels. The number of EREs is not calculated equally across all power:
subsidies.artikel-t1-head: <th style="padding:0.5rem 0.75rem;text-align:left;">Energy source</th><th style="padding:0.5rem 0.75rem;text-align:left;">Share that counts</th><th style="padding:0.5rem 0.75rem;text-align:left;">Revenue per 1,000 kWh</th>
subsidies.artikel-t1-r1: Power from the grid50.5% (average green share, 2026)approx. €130
subsidies.artikel-t1-r2: Own solar power with GoOs100%approx. €200
subsidies.artikel-p13: The background: for grid power, the NEa uses the average green share of the Dutch electricity grid. In 2026 that is 50.5%, regardless of whether the hotel has a green or grey contract. Power from your own solar panels is different: with Guarantees of Origin (GoOs) it is demonstrably green and counts fully. The difference is a factor of two in ERE revenue per charged kWh.
subsidies.artikel-p14: For a hotel, this is a concrete business case: keeping the solar power generated during the day available for charging in the evening via a battery yields twice the EREs per kWh. The energy management system plays a steering role in this. A hotel that sets up this combination well lets its solar panels pay back in two ways: on the energy bill and on the ERE revenue.
subsidies.artikel-h3-7: How the sale of EREs is organised
subsidies.artikel-p15: Hotels cannot trade EREs themselves; only NEa-recognised booking service providers may register and sell. Dozens of parties are active in the Netherlands. A few criteria are decisive when choosing a party (we deliberately mention no names):
subsidies.artikel-li14: Recognition by the NEa as a booking service provider.
subsidies.artikel-li15: Commission on the revenue, typically 13% to 19%, sometimes decreasing over the years.
subsidies.artikel-li16: Payout rhythm: quarterly or annually, and whether a guaranteed minimum per kWh applies.
subsidies.artikel-li17: Contract form: usually a calendar-year contract with a short notice period.
subsidies.artikel-li18: Transparency: reporting on volumes sold and price achieved, plus clear audit costs.
subsidies.artikel-h3-8: Worked example: a hotel with sixteen charge points
subsidies.artikel-p16: A realistic picture: sixteen AC charge points (11 or 22 kW), on average one charging session of 25 kWh per charge point per working day. That comes to 100,000 kWh per year.
subsidies.artikel-li19: ERE revenue: approximately 25,000 to 33,000 EREs per year (depending on the counting factor: the NEa method with 50.5% counting gives around 25,000 EREs; some providers use a higher factor).
subsidies.artikel-li20: Without solar panels (50.5% counts, net after commission): approximately €10,000 to €13,000 per year.
subsidies.artikel-li21: With solar panels and GoOs (100% counts): approximately €20,000 per year, up to twice as much as on grid power.
subsidies.artikel-li22: Per 1,000 charged kWh: approximately €100 to €130 net on grid power, approximately €200 on own solar power.
subsidies.artikel-p17: For hotels that have to install charging infrastructure anyway (the EPBD IV directive increasingly requires it), this is no side issue: the ERE revenue pays back a substantial part of the investment.
subsidies.artikel-h3-9: The simple calculation: one charge point, four hours a day
subsidies.artikel-p18: For a first estimate, a simple calculation suffices. One 11 kW charge point used on average four hours a day:
subsidies.artikel-t2-head: <th style="padding:0.5rem 0.75rem;text-align:left;">Situation</th><th style="padding:0.5rem 0.75rem;text-align:left;">Revenue per year</th><th style="padding:0.5rem 0.75rem;text-align:left;">Per day</th>
subsidies.artikel-t2-r2: With solar panels and GoOs (100%)approx. €3,200approx. €8.80
subsidies.artikel-callout2: The rule of thumb: count on €0.12 net per charged kWh on grid power and €0.20 on own solar power. A hotel with ten charge points therefore reaches €19,000 to €32,000 per year, depending on the energy source.

subsidies.faq-h2: Frequently asked questions about subsidies for your hotel
subsidies.faq-q1: How much subsidy can my hotel get?
subsidies.faq-a1: It depends on the measure: EIA gives a 40% fiscal deduction on energy investments, MIA/Vamil gives extra deduction and free depreciation on the environmental list, ISDE subsidises heat pumps, and SPRILA contributes to chargers on your own grounds. On top of that, every charged kWh generates a recurring income stream through EREs. Calculate in the energy configurator what your hotel can save.
subsidies.faq-q2: Subsidy for a battery in my hotel?
subsidies.faq-a2: A commercial battery (ESS) qualifies for EIA and, if the system is on the environmental list, for MIA/Vamil. The battery stores solar power, cuts peaks and keeps power available for charging. Explore Lemnion's battery solutions.
subsidies.faq-q3: Subsidy for EV chargers in my hotel?
subsidies.faq-a3: The hotel scheme is SPRILA: subsidy per charge point on own or leased grounds, for guests and staff. On top of that, every charged kWh generates EREs. Read how EREs let your chargers pay themselves back.
subsidies.faq-q4: Subsidy for solar panels in my hotel?
subsidies.faq-a4: Solar panels qualify fiscally through EIA and MIA/Vamil. Note: ISDE does not subsidise solar panels for businesses, but it does subsidise heat pumps and solar boilers. Read how to become gas-free without grid reinforcement.
subsidies.faq-q5: How do I combine subsidies with EREs?
subsidies.faq-a5: Subsidies lower the investment upfront; EREs generate annual income per charged kWh. With solar panels and a battery, you double that ERE revenue, because own solar power counts for 100%. The combination makes the business case for charging infrastructure strong: a lower investment, a higher annual return.
subsidies.faq-q6: Does my hotel need an energy label?
subsidies.faq-a6: For utility buildings larger than 1,000 m², including hotels, a minimum energy label C has applied since 2023. In addition, the EPBD IV directive obliges many hotels to install charging infrastructure. Read everything about the EPBD IV obligation. Lemnion can determine with an energy scan where your hotel stands and which route leads to the label.
